brief.scenario: Jamie Studley, 10, has abdominal pain that has become localised to the right lower quadrant, with anorexia and vomiting.
brief.task: Discuss your differential, assessment and management with the examiner.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Systematic assessment with analgesia throughout, not a diagnosis from one sign.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Treating vomiting as proof of gastroenteritis, or withholding analgesia to protect the diagnosis.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd take a focused history and examine him, making sure he has appropriate analgesia throughout."

grid.label: Approach to the child and family
grid.fail: Speaks only to the parent and does not address the child at all.
grid.pass: Involves Jamie directly at his level while also including his parent or carer.
grid.high: Adapts language to his age and checks understanding with both Jamie and his parent.

grid.label: Differential diagnosis
grid.fail: Assumes gastroenteritis because he vomited, or names only appendicitis.
grid.pass: Differentiates gastroenteritis, mesenteric adenitis, constipation, urinary pathology and other surgical causes.
grid.high: Adds testicular examination in a boy and pregnancy-related differentials in an adolescent girl, not relying on one sign alone.

grid.label: Focused assessment
grid.fail: Does not ask about pain migration, anorexia or fever, or skips examining for peritonism.
grid.pass: Asks about pain migration, anorexia, vomiting, fever and bowel/urinary symptoms, and examines for guarding and peritonism.
grid.high: States peritonism or sepsis requires urgent surgical assessment rather than routine review.

grid.label: Analgesia (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Withholds or delays analgesia, believing it will mask signs.
grid.pass: Ensures appropriate analgesia is given while assessment continues, and explains it does not mask serious disease.
grid.high: Cites that analgesia does not delay diagnosis and reassures the family accordingly.

grid.label: Investigation strategy
grid.fail: States every child with abdominal pain needs a CT scan.
grid.pass: Uses investigations according to the clinical picture and local paediatric pathway, with ultrasound first-line.
grid.high: Explains CT is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty because of radiation exposure in children.

grid.label: Escalation and safety-netting
grid.fail: Manages him alone without involving paediatric surgery despite suspecting appendicitis.
grid.pass: Involves the paediatric surgical team when appendicitis is suspected.
grid.high: Adds that ongoing reassessment, not a single review, may be needed if the diagnosis remains uncertain.

pass.text: This is Jamie, 10, with pain that's moved to the right lower quadrant, off his food and vomiting. What's going through your mind?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd introduce myself to Jamie and his mum, explain things simply to him, and make sure she understands too.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Appendicitis, gastroenteritis, mesenteric adenitis, constipation, urinary tract infection and other surgical causes.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd ask about pain migration, anorexia, vomiting, fever, bowel and urinary symptoms, then examine for guarding and peritonism.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd make sure he has appropriate analgesia while I assess him - withholding it isn't necessary.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd use investigations according to the clinical picture and our local paediatric pathway.

pass.speaker: candidate

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: This is Jamie, 10, with pain that's moved to the right lower quadrant, off his food and vomiting. What's going through your mind?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd introduce myself to both of them, use language Jamie can follow, and check he and his mum have both understood.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Appendicitis, gastroenteritis, mesenteric adenitis, constipation, urinary pathology and other surgical causes - and in a boy I'd also consider testicular pathology, since no single sign rules anything out.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: History of pain migration, anorexia, vomiting, fever, bowel and urinary symptoms, then careful examination; if there's peritonism I'd treat that as needing urgent surgical assessment.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He should have appropriate analgesia throughout - it won't mask a surgical abdomen or delay diagnosis, and I'd reassure his mum of that.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Pathway-based imaging, ultrasound first-line; I'd reserve CT for genuine diagnostic uncertainty given the radiation exposure in a child.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Paediatric surgery promptly if appendicitis is suspected, and I'd keep reassessing him rather than relying on one review if things stay unclear.

failures.move: Withholding analgesia because it might mask signs.
failures.consequence: The child is left in unnecessary pain without improving diagnostic accuracy.

failures.move: Requesting CT in every child with abdominal pain.
failures.consequence: Exposes children to unnecessary radiation when ultrasound and clinical review would suffice.

failures.move: Assuming vomiting means gastroenteritis without considering surgical causes.
failures.consequence: A surgical abdomen such as appendicitis can be missed or its recognition delayed.

failures.move: Managing suspected appendicitis without involving paediatric surgery.
failures.consequence: Delays definitive assessment and operative treatment if it is needed.

recovery.when: You realise you've assumed a diagnosis too early
recovery.line: I'd like to step back and work through the differential systematically.
Appropriate analgesia should be given; it does not mask a surgical abdomen.

knowledge.fact: Appendicitis in children typically presents with pain migrating towards the right iliac fossa, anorexia, vomiting and localised peritonism.
Analgesia should not be withheld in children with suspected appendicitis; it does not mask serious disease.
Ultrasound is first-line imaging for suspected paediatric appendicitis; CT is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty.
The differential includes gastroenteritis, mesenteric adenitis, constipation, urinary pathology, testicular pathology in boys and pregnancy-related causes in adolescent girls.

recall.think: Missing a surgical abdomen while treating pain relief as something to be earned.
recall.say: "Suspected appendicitis - analgesia now, paediatric surgical review."
do: Ask about migration, anorexia, vomiting, fever
Analgesia; involve paediatric surgery if suspected

numbers.meaning: Low/intermediate/high-risk stratification used to decide who needs ultrasound imaging

recall.trap: Assuming a vomiting child obviously has gastroenteritis.
recall.finish: Paediatric surgical involvement and pathway-based imaging, not a reflex CT.

partner.opening: Jamie, 10, has pain that has moved to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia and vomiting. What is your differential and how would you assess and manage him?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the pain pattern
reveals.finding: Pain started around the umbilicus yesterday and has now settled in the right lower quadrant.
Localised tenderness and guarding in the right iliac fossa; no rebound elicited yet.

push.question: Should you withhold analgesia until surgery is more certain?
push.expect: No - appropriate analgesia should be given; it does not mask a surgical abdomen.

push.question: Does every child with this presentation need a CT?
push.expect: No - ultrasound first-line per pathway; CT only for diagnostic uncertainty.

push.question: Who should be told about him?
push.expect: The paediatric surgical team, promptly, given suspected appendicitis.

curveballs.prompt: The patient is actually a 14-year-old girl with the same presentation.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Include pregnancy-related and gynaecological differentials alongside the standard differential.

curveballs.prompt: His mother says he's 'always dramatic' and asks you to send him home.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explain that assessment findings, not the parent's impression, guide the decision, and safety-net clearly if discharged.

curveballs.prompt: On examination there is generalised peritonism, not just localised tenderness.
curveballs.safeAnswer: This raises concern for perforation; arrange urgent surgical assessment rather than routine work-up.
